title: Overview of Retailing

pattern.summary: 8 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. All theory; Q8 is short notes (any two). Give Indian retail examples (Big Bazaar, DMart, Reliance Trends, Amazon) in every answer.

choosing: Retail formats, store management (location, layout, space performance), consumer behaviour, technology in retail and ethics come up in almost every paper.
Name real Indian retailers as examples — it is the easiest way to lift a theory answer.

topics.name: Retail Formats (Store, Non-store, Franchise, E-tailing)
topics.summary: Classification of formats, modern vs traditional, non-store retailing, franchising, e-tailing, cash and carry.
points: Traditional formats: kirana/mom-and-pop stores, haats and melas, street vendors, general stores.

Modern store formats: department store (Shoppers Stop), supermarket, hypermarket (Big Bazaar), convenience store, speciality store (Tanishq), discount store (DMart), category killer, factory outlet, malls, chain stores.
Modern vs traditional: organised, large, self-service, wide assortment, technology, standard prices vs small, owner-run, credit and personal service.
Non-store retailing: direct selling (Amway), catalogue shops, telemarketing, vending machines, TV shopping, e-tailing.
Cash and carry: wholesale self-service for registered businesses (Metro, Walmart Best Price).
Brick and mortar: physical stores; click and mortar: both physical and online.

Franchising: franchisor gives the brand and system, franchisee pays a fee/royalty. Types: product/trade-name, business-format, manufacturer–retailer. Merits: fast expansion, low capital for franchisor, proven model for franchisee. Limits: less control, royalty cost, dependence.
E-tailing: selling online (Amazon, Flipkart). Advantages: 24×7, wide reach, low cost, convenience. Limitations: no touch and feel, delivery and return issues, security concerns.

Choice of format follows location: department stores suit scarce central city space, hypermarkets need large plots on the outskirts, neighbourhoods suit food and daily-needs stores, high streets suit brand stores, and malls offer everything under one roof.
Emerging trends in the book: cash-and-carry, growth through mergers and acquisitions, and the rise of private brands changing the manufacturer–retailer relationship.
topics.frame: Meaning → classification chart (store / non-store) → each format with an Indian example → merits → conclusion.

units.title: Emerging Trends and Careers in Retail Industry

examples:
Examples: matching formats
The kirana shop on the corner (traditional, credit and personal service); a supermarket with self-service aisles; a hypermarket on the highway with groceries plus electronics; a jewellery speciality store; a discount store with everyday low prices; Amway distributors (direct selling, non-store); a vending machine at a station; a cash-and-carry wholesale store that only serves registered businesses.

topics.name: Retail Consumer Behaviour
topics.summary: Buyer vs consumer, factors influencing retail consumers, buying decision process, situational variables, store image, CRM.
points: Buyer purchases; consumer uses — may be different people.

Factors: cultural (culture, sub-culture, class), social (family, reference groups, role and status), personal (age, occupation, income, lifestyle), psychological (motivation, perception, learning, attitude).
Buying decision process: need recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase decision → post-purchase behaviour (e.g. buying a new car).
Situational variables: physical surroundings, social surroundings, time, task (gift or self), mood.
Store image: how consumers see a store — merchandise, price, service, ambience, location.
Customer relationship marketing: keeping customers through loyalty programmes, personalised offers and service.
Buying roles: initiator, influencer, decider, buyer and user — often the household, not one person, is the real target.

The book's four situational dimensions: physical setting, social setting, temporal (time) setting and task setting. Every store must communicate its own individuality (store image) to its target customers.
topics.frame: Meaning → factors or stages as headed points with a retail example → why retailers must understand it.
examples:
Example: situational variables change the purchase
The same shopper buys a cheap umbrella at a station kiosk when it suddenly rains (time pressure, physical surroundings), but a branded gift set after comparing stores when shopping for a friend's wedding (task: a gift, with social surroundings — friends along). The store's image — clean, helpful staff, fair prices — decides where she shops in the second case.

topics.name: Store Location, Layout, Display & Space
topics.summary: Store location factors, layouts, display, atmosphere, internal/external environment, space management and performance measures.
points: Location factors: target population and income, footfall and accessibility, competition, parking, rent and cost, visibility, zoning laws.
Layouts: grid (supermarkets), free-form (boutiques), racetrack/loop (department stores), spine, herringbone.
Display: window display, interior display, point-of-purchase displays, fixtures, signage, lighting.
Store atmosphere: lighting, colour, music, scent, temperature, cleanliness — shapes mood and time spent.
Internal environment: layout, display, ambience, staff. External: storefront, signage, parking, surroundings.
Space performance measures: sales per square foot, gross margin per square foot, GMROF, sales per linear foot of shelf, space productivity index.
Store space management: allocating space to categories by their sales and profit contribution.

Atmospherics has four parts in the book: exterior atmospherics (entrance, signboard, window display, parking), interior atmospherics (flooring, design, cleanliness), store layout (free-flow, grid, boutique) and visual merchandising.
topics.frame: Meaning → factors or types with a small layout sketch → examples → conclusion.
examples:
Example: layout and display decisions
A supermarket uses a grid layout with milk and bread at the back, so shoppers pass other aisles. A boutique uses a free-form layout to encourage browsing. A department store uses a racetrack loop leading past every department.
Impulse items such as chocolates sit at the billing counter (point-of-purchase display); soft lighting, music and a pleasant scent make customers stay longer.

topics.name: Growth, Trends & Challenges of Retail in India
topics.summary: Factors driving retail growth in India, global and Indian trends, challenges, future, liberalisation, rural retail.
points: Growth factors: rising incomes, young population, urbanisation, nuclear families, working women, credit and digital payments, FDI and liberalisation, growth of malls and e-commerce.
Trends: omnichannel, e-commerce and quick commerce, private labels, digital payments (UPI), data analytics, experiential stores, rural retail, sustainability.
Global trends: consolidation, omnichannel, automation, personalisation, green retail.
Challenges: high real-estate cost, poor infrastructure and supply chain, skilled-manpower shortage, complex regulations, competition from unorganised and online retail, shrinkage.
Liberalisation (1991 onwards): FDI in single- and multi-brand retail, entry of global players, better supply chains.
Rural retailing: large untapped market; e.g. ITC e-Choupal, Hariyali Kisaan Bazaar.

The book notes that retail is India's biggest employer after agriculture and that organised retail is still a small share (just over 10%) of sales; policy has tried to protect small unorganised retailers from big foreign chains.

Foreign entry has been bumpy: Walmart's venture with Bharti and Shoprite's with Nirmal Lifestyle broke up, while Indian players such as Reliance Retail grew fast. Congestion, high city rents, and labour and land laws hold organised retail back.
topics.frame: Headed points with Indian examples and a line on the future outlook.
examples:
Example: a trend in practice — omnichannel and quick commerce
A customer checks a shirt on a retailer's app, tries it in the store, finds her size out of stock, orders it from the store's tablet for home delivery, and pays by UPI. Meanwhile her groceries arrive in 15 minutes from a quick-commerce dark store. Rising incomes, smartphones and digital payments make both possible, while high rents and supply-chain gaps remain challenges.

topics.name: Ethics in Retailing
topics.summary: Business ethics in retail, ethical and non-ethical behaviour, benefits of managing ethics, the carry-bag charge issue.
points: Business ethics: moral principles guiding retail decisions.

Areas: with customers (honest pricing, fair weights, no misleading ads), suppliers (fair terms, timely payment), employees (fair wages, safety), competitors (fair competition), society and environment.
Non-ethical behaviour: misleading discounts, selling expired goods, hidden charges, bait-and-switch, poor treatment of staff, data misuse.
Benefits of managing ethics: customer trust and loyalty, reputation, employee morale, fewer legal problems, long-term profit.

Carry-bag charges: consumer forums have held that charging for branded carry bags without prior notice is an unfair trade practice — retailers should inform customers, offer free or eco-friendly bags, or allow customers to bring their own.

Ethical grey areas the book discusses: the carry-bag charge (settled in the courts), frisking customers at the exit, giving sweets instead of exact change, pushing impulse buys, and promoting offers that are already 'sold out'. Shoplifting shows the retailer is not always the one at fault.
topics.frame: Meaning → areas or behaviours as headed points with examples → benefits → conclusion.
examples:
Example: ethical and unethical practices
Unethical: raising the 'MRP' before announcing a 50% discount; selling goods near expiry without disclosure; charging for a branded carry bag without telling the customer first (held an unfair trade practice by consumer forums). Ethical: clear prices, honest weights, prompt payment to small suppliers, and fair wages and safety for staff — building trust that brings customers back.

topics.name: Technology in Retailing
topics.summary: Applications and trends of technology in retail, POS, SEO/SEM, harmful impacts and precautions, choosing technology.
points: Applications: POS systems and billing, barcodes and RFID, inventory management, ERP, CRM and loyalty, e-commerce and mobile apps, digital payments, self-checkout, CCTV and EAS tags, data analytics.
Trends: AI and personalisation, AR/VR try-ons, omnichannel, cashless and contactless payment, electronic shelf labels, robots in warehouses.
POS software: records sales, prints bills, updates stock, gives sales reports.
SEO (search engine optimisation): free ranking in search results. SEM (search engine marketing): paid ads in search results.
Harmful impact: job losses, high costs, data privacy and cyber risks, over-dependence, digital divide. Remedies: staff training, data security, phased adoption.
Factors for choosing technology: cost, scalability, ease of use, integration, vendor support, security.
The book warns that retail technology dates quickly, so a retailer must weigh its needs against the risk of buying something that is soon obsolete.
topics.frame: Meaning → applications as headed points with retailer examples → precautions → conclusion.
examples:
Example: technology from shelf to customer
RFID tags let staff count the whole store's stock in minutes; the POS system bills, updates stock and shows the day's best sellers; low stock triggers an automatic reorder in the ERP; the loyalty app sends a personalised coupon. Online, the store appears in free search results through SEO and buys search ads (SEM) during the festival sale.

topics.name: Merchandising & Visual Merchandising
topics.summary: Merchandising objectives and budget, merchandise mix, cross merchandising, visual merchandising, private vs national brands.
points: Merchandising: planning and managing the right product, at the right place, time, quantity and price.
Objectives: meet customer demand, maximise sales and margin, optimise stock, support store image.
Merchandise budget: planned sales, stock levels, reductions (markdowns, shrinkage), purchases, gross margin; constrained by funds, space, supplier terms, season.
Merchandise mix: width (number of categories), depth (items per category), consistency. Factors: target customers, store format, competition, space, season, margin.
Cross merchandising: displaying related products together (pasta with sauce) to raise basket size.
Visual merchandising: presenting products attractively — window displays, fixtures, lighting, colour, signage, mannequins, planograms.
Private brands (retailer's own, e.g. DMart's Premia) vs national brands (manufacturer's): higher margin and control vs strong pull and trust.
topics.frame: Meaning → components or factors as headed points → retailer examples → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a merchandise budget
Planned sales for October ₹10 lakh; planned reductions (markdowns and shrinkage) ₹1 lakh; desired closing stock ₹6 lakh; opening stock ₹5 lakh.
Planned purchases = 10 + 1 + 6 − 5 = ₹12 lakh.
Cross merchandising: pasta displayed with sauce and cheese raises the average bill; visual merchandising puts winter wear on mannequins at the entrance in November.

topics.name: Retailing: Meaning, Functions & Structural Change
topics.summary: Meaning and functions of a retailer, success factors, theories of structural change, careers in retail.
points: Retailing: selling goods and services directly to final consumers for personal use.
Functions: assortment, breaking bulk, holding stock, services (credit, delivery), information to producers and customers, creating convenience.
Success factors: understanding customers, right location, merchandise and price, service, technology, cost control.

Theories of structural change: wheel of retailing (new formats enter low-cost, trade up, leave space for new low-cost entrants), retail accordion (general → specialised → general assortment), retail life cycle (innovation, growth, maturity, decline), dialectic process (thesis + antithesis → synthesis).
Employment options: store operations (sales associate, store manager), merchandising and buying, visual merchandising, supply chain, marketing, e-commerce, HR and finance.
Newer retail careers named in the book: category management, data analytics, CRM and loyalty, trend analysis and competition screening, plus the growing online-retail roles.
topics.frame: Definition → points with headings → diagram for the wheel of retailing → conclusion.

units.title: Emerging Trends and Careers in Retail Industry

examples:
Example: the wheel of retailing
A discount chain enters with bare stores, few services and very low prices. As it grows, it adds air-conditioning, trial rooms, home delivery and a loyalty programme — costs and prices rise. That leaves room for a new low-price entrant (now often an online seller) to repeat the cycle.

topics.name: Security, Finance & Performance in Retail
topics.summary: Security arrangements and shrinkage, financial planning, performance measurement and retail audit.
points: Shrinkage: loss of stock through shoplifting, employee theft, administrative errors, vendor fraud and damage.
Security measures: CCTV, EAS tags and gates, security guards, mirrors, locked cases, staff checks, cash controls — they deter theft and reduce losses.
Financial planning: budgeting sales, costs and capital; inventory valuation; working capital and cash flow; pricing for margin.
Performance measures: sales per sq ft, GMROI, inventory turnover, conversion rate, average transaction value, same-store sales growth.
Retail audit: systematic check of operations, stock, finance and compliance.
Retail audits in the book: store operations audit, inventory audit, financial (commercial) audit and customer-service audit — done internally and externally.
CRM keeps customers coming back through membership cards, loyalty and referral programmes; performance is tracked with KRAs and score cards.
topics.frame: Meaning → measures as headed points → conclusion.
examples:
Example: retail performance measures
Annual sales ₹1.2 crore from a 4,000 sq ft store → ₹3,000 per sq ft.
Gross margin ₹30 lakh on average inventory (at cost) of ₹10 lakh → GMROI 3 (each rupee of stock earns ₹3 of margin).
On one day 1,000 people enter and 250 buy → conversion rate 25%; sales ₹5 lakh ÷ 250 bills → average transaction value ₹2,000.
Shrinkage from shoplifting is controlled with EAS tags, CCTV and bag checks.

topics.name: Sourcing & Supplier Selection
topics.summary: Meaning of sourcing, global sourcing decisions, evaluating and selecting suppliers.
points: Sourcing: finding and choosing suppliers of merchandise.
Global sourcing factors: cost and exchange rates, quality, lead time, duties and trade rules, political stability, logistics, supplier reliability.
Supplier evaluation criteria: price, quality, reliability of delivery, financial stability, capacity, flexibility, after-sales support, ethics and compliance.
Comparative evaluation: weighted scoring of suppliers on these criteria.
topics.frame: Meaning → factors as headed points → a small weighted-score table → conclusion.
examples:
Example: weighted scoring of two suppliers
Weights: price 40%, quality 30%, delivery 20%, service 10%.
Supplier A scores 8, 7, 9, 6 → 3.2 + 2.1 + 1.8 + 0.6 = 7.7.
Supplier B scores 9, 6, 6, 8 → 3.6 + 1.8 + 1.2 + 0.8 = 7.4.
A wins although B is cheaper, because of better quality and delivery.

topics.name: Retail Laws, GST & VAT
topics.summary: Acts governing retail, Consumer Protection Act, GST and its benefits, VAT.
points: Acts: Consumer Protection Act (1986, replaced in 2019), Shops and Establishments Act, Legal Metrology Act (weights and measures), Food Safety and Standards Act, Sale of Goods Act, GST Act, Trade Marks Act, labour laws.
Consumer Protection Act: consumer rights (safety, information, choice, to be heard, redressal, education); consumer commissions at district, state and national levels.
GST (2017): one indirect tax replacing VAT, excise and service tax. Benefits for retail: no cascading tax, input tax credit, simpler compliance, easier inter-state movement, lower logistics cost.
VAT: state tax on value added at each stage (replaced by GST).
topics.frame: List the acts → explain three or four in detail with relevance to retail → conclusion.
examples:
Example: input tax credit under GST
A retailer buys a mixer for ₹1,000 + 18% GST (₹180) and sells it for ₹1,500 + 18% GST (₹270). It pays the government only ₹270 − ₹180 = ₹90, the tax on its value addition of ₹500. Before GST, taxes at different stages could pile up as tax on tax (cascading).
A customer sold a mixer that breaks in a week can complain to the District Consumer Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

topics.name: Retail Pricing
topics.summary: Methods of setting retail prices, EDLP, psychological pricing.
points: Methods: cost-oriented (mark-up), demand-oriented, competition-oriented.
Strategies: everyday low pricing (EDLP — DMart, Walmart), high-low pricing (frequent promotions), odd/psychological pricing (₹99), prestige pricing, loss leaders, bundle pricing, price lining.
Psychological pricing: prices set to influence perception — ₹499 feels cheaper than ₹500.
examples:
Example: mark-up and pricing strategies
Cost ₹400; mark-up 25% on cost → price ₹500. The same ₹100 is a 20% mark-up on the selling price (100 ÷ 500).
Psychological pricing: ₹499 instead of ₹500. Loss leader: sugar sold at cost to bring shoppers in. EDLP: steady low prices every day. High-low: higher regular prices with frequent sales. Bundle: shampoo + conditioner pack at ₹299.
